lesson.title: Six Ways to Compare: Beyond == and <
lesson.summary: Python supports six comparison operators, each backed by its own dunder method, and functools.total_ordering can fill in the remaining ones once a class defines __eq__ and just one ordering method.
lesson.body:
The previous chapter on __eq__ and __lt__ methods showed how to make == and < mean something specific for a custom class. Those are two of six comparison operators Python supports: == and !=, backed by __eq__ and __ne__; < and >, backed by __lt__ and __gt__; and <= and >=, backed by __le__ and __ge__. Unlike arithmetic operators, Python does not automatically derive the other four just because you defined __eq__ and __lt__. Try it directly:

```python
class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.cents == other.cents

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.cents < other.cents

a = Money(500)
b = Money(500)
print(a <= b)
```

This raises a TypeError, because Money has no __le__ (and no __ge__ for Python to try as a fallback either), so there is nothing that knows how to answer a <= b. Sorting and min()/max() only ever need __lt__, which is why sorted() worked fine in the previous chapter without any of the other four operators being defined, but <= specifically needs a method of its own.

Writing all four remaining comparison methods by hand for every ordered class would be repetitive and error-prone, so the standard library provides a shortcut: the total_ordering class decorator from the functools module. Given a class that defines __eq__ and at least one of __lt__, __le__, __gt__, or __ge__, total_ordering fills in the rest automatically, built out of the ones you already wrote.

```python
from functools import total_ordering

@total_ordering
class Money:
    def __init__(self, cents):
        self.cents = cents

    def __eq__(self, other):
        return self.cents == other.cents

    def __lt__(self, other):
        return self.cents < other.cents

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"${self.cents / 100:.2f}"

prices = [Money(999), Money(150), Money(500)]
print(sorted(prices))
print(Money(500) <= Money(500))
print(Money(150) > Money(500))
```

This prints [$1.50, $5.00, $9.99], then True, then False. sorted() still only needed __lt__, exactly as before. Money(500) <= Money(500) is True: total_ordering's generated __le__ combines the __lt__ and __eq__ you already wrote, and 500 is equal to 500. Money(150) > Money(500) is False, since the generated __gt__ checks that 150 is not less than 500 and that the two amounts are not equal, and 150 is in fact less than 500, so neither condition needed for "greater than" holds.

It is good practice, though not required for these examples to run, for a custom __eq__ to guard against being compared to a completely unrelated type. If other were, say, a string instead of a Money object, self.cents == other.cents would raise an AttributeError rather than sensibly returning False. The conventional fix is to check the type first and return the special value NotImplemented when the comparison does not make sense, which tells Python to ask the other object whether it knows how to compare itself to a Money, before giving up entirely, rather than crashing outright.

This chapter connects directly back to the previous one on object identity: identity, checked with is, is not one of the six comparison operators, and it cannot be customized with a dunder method at all. Equality and ordering, by contrast, are entirely up to the class: __eq__ and its five companions decide what "equal," "less than," and "at least as large as" mean for objects that, as far as Python's default identity check is concerned, are still separate things sitting in separate places in memory.
